result.title: Full-URL allowlist/denylist patterns matched by raw string prefix, allowing a domain-restriction bypass
result.defect:
In `_is_url_match` (security_watchdog.py, original lines 282-287), a "full URL" pattern (any pattern containing `'://'`, e.g. `allowed_domains=['https://example.com']`) was checked with a plain string comparison: `if url.startswith(pattern): return True`. Since `'https://example.com'` is a literal string prefix of `'https://example.com.evil.com'` and even of `'https://example.comevil.com'`, both of those completely different, attacker-controlled hosts were treated as allowed — there was no host-boundary check between the pattern's host and whatever the actual URL's host continued with. Verified live against the unfixed code:
```
allowed_domains=['https://example.com']
_is_url_allowed('https://example.com.evil.com/path') -> True   # should be False
_is_url_allowed('https://example.comevil.com/path')  -> True   # should be False
```
This is exactly the bypass class the task calls out as highest-value for this file: an agent configured with an allowlist could be redirected (e.g. via a same-site open redirect, an ad, or a compromised link) to `https://example.com.attacker.com` and SecurityWatchdog would wave it through as if it were the allowed `example.com`. The same raw-prefix logic is used for `prohibited_domains` too, so it's also under-blocking there (a prohibited full URL pattern doesn't reliably block, though the more severe direction is the allow-list bypass).
result.self_critique:
Checked the alternatives before touching anything:
- Not intentional: the field docstring in `browser/profile.py` documents `"https://example.com"` as a plain per-domain example (like `"*.google.com"`), not as a deliberate "any-host-with-this-string-prefix" wildcard mechanism — that's what the `*` glob branch is explicitly for, and glob patterns are handled in a completely separate code path just above this one. There's no comment anywhere suggesting `startswith` was meant to do host-prefix matching across host boundaries; it's a leftover artifact of treating a URL pattern as an opaque string.
- Not already covered: grepped `tests/ci/security/test_domain_filtering.py` (571 lines) — it has a `test_www_subdomain_not_added_for_url_patterns` test that only checks `'https://example.com/path'` (path continuation under the *same* host) and never a differing/attacker host sharing the pattern as a string prefix. No existing test exercises this.
- Compatibility: the fix only changes behavior for URLs whose host is a strict superset-string of an allowed/prohibited pattern's host but is actually a *different* host (the exploit case) — it does not change matching for the same host with a deeper path, which I explicitly re-verified still works (`'https://good.com/some/path'` continuing to `'https://good.com/some/path/deeper'`). Existing test suite (105 tests in `tests/ci/security/` + `tests/ci/test_registry_empty_url_domain_filter.py`) still passes unchanged, confirming no observable regression in any previously-relied-upon behavior.
- Simpler explanation ruled out: could this be "intentionally lenient because block_ip_addresses/other checks catch it elsewhere"? No — those are separate, independent checks (IP literal detection, credential-in-URL host confusion) that don't touch hostname-suffix continuation at all; nothing else in the file re-validates host equality for full-URL patterns.
This is a solid, exploitable finding, not a stylistic nit, so I implemented the fix rather than discarding it.
result.fix_summary: In the exact-match branch of `_is_url_match` for full URL patterns (containing `'://'`), parse the pattern itself with `urlparse` and require that the incoming URL's `scheme` and `host` match the pattern's scheme/hostname *exactly* (case-insensitive host compare, consistent with the rest of the file) before falling back to a `startswith` check — and that `startswith` check now only decides whether a pattern-specified *path* additionally constrains the match (since the host is already proven equal at that point, a plain prefix check on the full string is safe for the path portion). If the pattern has no path (or just `/`), any path under the matched host is allowed, matching prior behavior for e.g. `'https://example.com'` matching `'https://example.com/path'`. No change to the glob-pattern branch or the domain-only exact-match branch (those already do host-only, not string-prefix, comparisons).

result.title: MCPClient reconnect silently tears the session back down (stale, already-set asyncio.Event)
result.defect:
`MCPClient.__init__` (line 77) creates `self._disconnect_event = asyncio.Event()` exactly once, for the object's whole lifetime. `_run_stdio_client` (line 153) uses it to keep the stdio/session context managers open: `await self._disconnect_event.wait()`. `disconnect()` (line 176) calls `self._disconnect_event.set()` but never resets it afterward, and `connect()` never creates a new one either.

Consequence: `connect() -> disconnect() -> connect()` (an ordinary reconnect/retry pattern the class is built to support -- `connect()` is idempotent via the `if self._connected: return` guard, and `disconnect()` is a public method, not just internal `__aexit__` plumbing) starts a fresh `_run_stdio_client` task whose `await self._disconnect_event.wait()` returns immediately because the *same* Event object is still in the `set()` state from the previous disconnect. That immediately exits the `async with stdio_client(...)` / `async with ClientSession(...)` blocks, closing the just-opened subprocess and session. `connect()`'s own polling loop (lines 101-109) only checks the *_connected* flag, so it happens to observe the brief `True` window and returns successfully -- the caller has no way to know the connection is already gone. Any subsequent MCP tool call then fails with `\"MCP server '...' not connected\"` (line 312/362), contradicting connect()'s own docstring/contract (\"Connect to the MCP server and discover available tools\").

Reproduced live before the fix (tests/ci/_mcp_servers/echo_server.py as a real stdio MCP server, no mocks):
```
connected True ['echo']
disconnected False
reconnected? True
still connected after reconnect? False None
```
result.self_critique:
Checked whether this could be intentional or already covered:
- Is it actually wrong, or intentional single-use-only design? Nothing in the docstring, class comment, or usage (`__aenter__`/`__aexit__`, `register_to_tools`) suggests MCPClient is meant to be single-use. `disconnect()` is a normal public method, and there's no assertion or guard against calling `connect()` again afterward -- the `if self._connected: return` at the top of `connect()` is precisely the kind of guard you'd write to make reconnection safe, which makes the omission of resetting the event look like an oversight, not a deliberate one-shot design.
- Does an existing test cover it? Grepped all of `tests/` for `MCPClient(` / `StdioServerParameters` / `stdio_client` -- only `tests/ci/test_mcp_client_error_result.py` touches `MCPClient`, and it does so by hand-constructing an already-`_connected = True` mock session, bypassing `connect()`/`disconnect()`/`_run_stdio_client()` entirely. No test exercises a real connect/disconnect/reconnect cycle.
- Would the fix break documented/public behavior? No. It only replaces a stale internal `asyncio.Event` with a fresh one at the start of `connect()`; the public API (`connect`, `disconnect`, `register_to_tools`, context-manager use) is unchanged, and single connect-then-disconnect-once lifecycles (the common case, and what `__aenter__`/`__aexit__` do) are unaffected since they never call `connect()` a second time.
- Simpler explanation I might be missing: could this be "working as intended" because real agents never reconnect a given `MCPClient` instance, only ever `connect()` once per instance? Possible in practice, but that's not what the code enforces or documents, and it's a realistic scenario for any retry/resilience logic layered on top of `MCPClient` (e.g., an agent that disconnects a flaky server and reconnects later) -- exactly the kind of thing that would "visibly break a real agent session" as the task asks for. I'm confident this is real and worth fixing over chasing something shakier in the same file.
result.fix_summary: In `MCPClient.connect()`, before starting the stdio task, reassign `self._disconnect_event = asyncio.Event()` to get a fresh, unset event for this connection attempt, instead of relying on the one instantiated once in `__init__`. This makes `disconnect()` followed by `connect()` produce a session that actually stays up until the next `disconnect()`, matching the method's contract.

result.title: SchemaOptimizer silently collapses free-form dict fields into always-empty objects
result.defect:
`SchemaOptimizer.create_optimized_json_schema` (browser_use/llm/schema.py) is the shared JSON-schema builder used by every LLM provider (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Groq, DeepSeek, Mistral, litellm, oci_raw, vercel, azure, orcarouter, aws bedrock) to build the tool/structured-output schema for `output_format` models (docstring's own claim, line 20/28: "Also ensures OpenAI strict mode compatibility" / "strict mode compatibility").

Two places unconditionally force `additionalProperties: False` on every `type: object` node, regardless of whether that object actually has defined `properties`:
- line 45 (old): `skip_fields = ['additionalProperties', '$defs']` drops the original `additionalProperties` value for every object.
- lines 142-144 (old): `if optimized.get('type') == 'object': optimized['additionalProperties'] = False` — added unconditionally.
- lines 176-178 (old, `ensure_additional_properties_false`): a second, redundant sweep does the exact same thing over the whole tree.

Pydantic represents a free-form mapping field (`dict`, `dict[str, Any]`, `dict[str, X]`) as `{"type": "object", "additionalProperties": true (or a value schema), ...}` with NO `properties` key (verified: `M.model_json_schema()` for `metadata: dict[str, Any] = {}` gives `{"additionalProperties": true, "type": "object", ...}`). After the optimizer runs, that becomes `{"type": "object", "additionalProperties": false}` with no `properties` — which, under JSON Schema semantics, is satisfiable ONLY by `{}`. Any real key the model tries to report for that field is now invalid against its own advertised schema, so under a provider that enforces the schema (Anthropic tool-use, OpenAI strict structured outputs, Gemini function-calling) the field can never actually carry data — a silent, provider-wide data-loss bug, not a hypothetical.

This is concretely reachable through `browser_use/tools/extraction/schema_utils.py::_resolve_type` (line 63-67): a user-supplied extraction schema field of `{"type": "object"}` with no nested `properties` (a common way to ask "extract these as arbitrary key/value pairs") is turned into a bare `dict`-typed pydantic field, which is then passed straight into `create_optimized_json_schema` for the structured-extraction LLM call — exactly the pattern this bug corrupts.

Corroborating evidence that this is a real, known-but-unfixed limitation rather than intended design: `browser_use/tools/views.py` lines 70-74 contain an explicit comment documenting this exact failure mode and routing around it by encoding `WebMCPCallAction.arguments` as a JSON *string* instead of a `dict`, specifically "because a free-form `dict` field becomes `additionalProperties: false` under OpenAI strict structured output, which would leave the model unable to name any key at all." That workaround treats one call site; it does not fix the shared schema builder, so any other model or action with a genuine `dict[str, X]` field (including the extraction schema path above) still hits it.
result.self_critique:
Alternative explanations considered and ruled out:
1. "Intentional, for OpenAI strict-mode compliance" — OpenAI's strict mode genuinely cannot represent an arbitrary-keys object, but the correct response to that constraint is either to reject/flag such fields for that one provider, or (as the codebase itself already does for WebMCPCallAction) route the value through a JSON string. Silently rewriting the schema into one that can only ever validate `{}` is not "compatibility," it's semantic corruption, and it applies uniformly to every provider through this single shared function — including Anthropic, Gemini, Groq, DeepSeek, litellm, etc., none of which require closed objects and which happily accept `additionalProperties: true` or a typed value schema in their tool/function schemas. So even granting the OpenAI-strict rationale, the blanket application to all providers is wrong.
2. "Already covered by an existing test" — checked `tests/ci/models/test_llm_schema_optimizer.py` (the sibling test file for this exact module) and `browser_use/llm/tests/test_mistral_schema.py`; neither constructs a model with a bare `dict`/`dict[str, Any]` field, so nothing exercises this path. Confirmed by writing the regression test and watching it fail cleanly on unpatched code with a clear assertion message.
3. "Fixing it breaks documented/public behavior" — checked: (a) all currently-passing tests for this module still pass unchanged; (b) `_make_strict_compatible` (which forces `required` to include every property) is guarded by `'properties' in schema`, so it never touches a bare-dict node either way, no interaction; (c) the fix only changes behavior for objects with NO `properties` key, i.e. exactly the case that was previously broken — modeled objects (the only case any existing test or documented example touches) are byte-for-byte unaffected, verified by rerunning `test_llm_schema_optimizer.py`, `test_structured_extraction.py`, `test_webmcp.py`, `test_registry_validation.py`, and the full `tests/ci` suite.
4. "Maybe there's a simpler root cause I'm missing" — traced the exact two lines responsible (the `skip_fields` drop plus the two blanket "force False" passes) and confirmed with a minimal repro (`M.model_json_schema()` before/after `SchemaOptimizer.create_optimized_json_schema`) that the value is dropped and replaced, not merely reordered or renamed elsewhere.

The one honest weak point: OpenAI's own *strict* structured-output mode still cannot represent a genuinely open-ended dict even with this fix (that's a hard constraint of that one provider's strict schema dialect, not something `schema.py` can paper over) — my fix restores the schema to be *correct* for every provider that can represent it (which is most of them, and is exactly what pydantic itself already says the field means), rather than pretending OpenAI-strict works when it fundamentally cannot for this shape. That's a strictly better, less-wrong state than "silently force it to `{}` for everyone," and it doesn't regress any currently-tested behavior.
result.fix_summary:
In `SchemaOptimizer.create_optimized_json_schema` (browser_use/llm/schema.py):
1. No longer unconditionally strips the original `additionalProperties` value; it's captured (`had_additional_properties` / `original_additional_properties`) per schema node before being dropped from the initial pass.
2. When emitting the optimized node: if the object has non-empty `properties` (a modeled object), `additionalProperties: False` is still forced, exactly as before — this preserves OpenAI-strict compatibility for every existing action/model and is untouched behavior. If the object has NO `properties` (a free-form `dict`/mapping field), the original `additionalProperties` value is restored (recursively optimized if it was itself a schema dict, e.g. `dict[str, SomeModel]`) instead of being forced to `False`.
3. The redundant second sweep (`ensure_additional_properties_false`) was doing the same blanket overwrite and would have silently undone the fix; it's now gated the same way (`obj.get('type') == 'object' and obj.get('properties')`), so it no longer stomps on a free-form mapping's restored `additionalProperties`.

Net effect: modeled objects (everything every current test and action touches) are byte-identical to before. Bare `dict`/`dict[str, X]` fields now keep a usable schema (`additionalProperties: true` or the original value-type schema) instead of being collapsed into an object that can only ever be `{}`.

result.title: attach_to_target returned early on every tab after the first, silently disabling network-based download/PDF detection for all subsequent tabs
result.defect:
`DownloadsWatchdog.attach_to_target()` (called once per tab, on every `TabCreatedEvent` — see `browser_use/browser/session.py:2148` and `:1090`) had, at the original lines 489-491:

```python
if self._download_cdp_session_setup:
    self.logger.debug('[DownloadsWatchdog] Download listener already set up for browser session')
    return
```

`_download_cdp_session_setup` is a browser-session-wide flag (correctly, since `Browser.setDownloadBehavior` + the `downloadWillBegin`/`downloadProgress` CDP handlers only need registering once — see the comment directly above it). But the `return` didn't just skip that one-time registration block: it returned out of the *entire* `attach_to_target` coroutine, which meant the trailing line at the end of the function:

```python
# Set up network monitoring for this target (catches ALL download variants)
await self._setup_network_monitoring(target_id)
```

was never reached for any tab after the first. `_setup_network_monitoring` is explicitly per-target — it's what adds `target_id` to `self._network_monitored_targets`, which is what the global `Network.responseReceived` callback (`on_response_received`, defined inside `_setup_network_monitoring`) checks before inspecting a response's headers/mime-type for PDFs or `Content-Disposition: attachment`. Its own docstring says it "catches ALL download variants" — direct PDF navigation without a `.pdf` URL, iframes, JS-triggered downloads, any attachment header — none of which the URL-pattern-only `check_for_pdf_viewer` path can catch on its own.

Net effect: on any real multi-tab session (the common case — the agent opens new tabs constantly), only the first tab ever created gets network-based download/PDF auto-detection. Every tab opened afterward silently loses that capability, with no error, warning, or user-visible signal — directly contradicting `_setup_network_monitoring`'s own stated contract and the module's whole purpose ("PDF auto-download detection ... during browsing").

Fix: keep the log line (still useful, tracks that the one-time listener registration was skipped) but don't return from the function; let control fall through to the (already correctly-guarded) `if not self._download_cdp_session_setup:` block below it and then to `await self._setup_network_monitoring(target_id)`. That inner `if not self._download_cdp_session_setup:` block already exists and is what actually prevents double-registering the CDP-level handlers, so removing the early `return` doesn't reintroduce duplicate registration — it only removes the accidental skip of the per-target call.
result.self_critique:
Case against: could the early return be intentional — i.e., is `_setup_network_monitoring` itself meant to run only once, browser-wide, just like the CDP handler registration, so skipping it for later tabs is by design? No: `_setup_network_monitoring` takes `target_id` as its sole positional argument, has its own independent early-return guard (`if target_id in self._network_monitored_targets: return`) which is *per-target*, and does target-scoped work (`get_or_create_cdp_session(target_id, ...)`, `Network.enable(session_id=...)`, and `self._network_monitored_targets.add(target_id)`). If it were meant to run once per browser, it wouldn't take a target_id, need a per-target dedup set, or need `Network.enable` on each target's own CDP session (CDP's `Network` domain is enabled per session, not process-wide). The function's own docstring and inline comment ("Set up network monitoring for this target") both say per-target. So this isn't a stylistic quirk of a shared one-time setup — it's a straightforward accidental `return` placed one line too early, almost certainly introduced when someone refactored the once-per-session CDP registration path and didn't notice the shared early exit swallowed the per-target call below it.

Does an existing test cover this? I checked `tests/ci/test_downloads_watchdog.py` (pure-function tests of `_should_auto_download_network_response`, no BrowserSession) and `tests/ci/test_remote_download_complete_callback.py` (single fake target via `model_construct`, never exercises a second tab). Neither creates two tabs, so neither could have caught this.

Would fixing it change documented/public behavior in a way that breaks compatibility? No — this is a private watchdog method (`_setup_network_monitoring`, leading underscore) with no public API surface change; the fix restores documented behavior ("catches ALL download variants") rather than changing it. Ran the full CI suite (1376 passed, 35 skipped, 1 pre-existing-and-confirmed-unrelated failure) to check for any behavioral regression from tabs now getting extra `Network.enable` calls — none surfaced.

Is there a simpler explanation I'm missing, e.g. is `Network.enable` idempotent/global so skipping it for later tabs was harmless because some other code path enables it for them anyway? I checked — nothing else in this file or `session.py` calls `Network.enable` for a target's session; `SecurityWatchdog`/`DOMWatchdog` don't do it either (grepped `Network.enable` — only this one call site). So there was no other path compensating for the skip.

I'm confident this is real, not intentional, not already covered, and safe to fix as a one-line change.
